gloss: An animal with feathers, two wings, and a beak.
examples: A *bird* hit the window and knocked itself out.
There were hundreds of *birds* sitting on the wire outside.
She keeps a *bird* in a cage by the kitchen window.

gloss: A large bird of prey with a hooked beak and very good eyesight.
examples: An *eagle* circled over the canyon for almost an hour.
Two bald *eagles* nest on the island every spring.
The *eagle* dropped out of the sky and grabbed a fish.

gloss: A medium-sized bird of prey that hunts small animals by day.
examples: A *hawk* was sitting on the fence post, watching the field.
*Hawks* around here go after squirrels and rabbits.
We saw a red-tailed *hawk* on the drive up.

gloss: A fast bird of prey with long pointed wings.
examples: A *falcon* can dive faster than any other bird.
The city has a pair of *falcons* nesting on the courthouse.
He trained the *falcon* to come back to his glove.

gloss: A night bird with large forward-facing eyes and a flat face.
examples: An *owl* was hooting somewhere behind the barn.
*Owls* hunt at night, so you rarely see them.
We found an *owl* pellet under the big pine.

gloss: A large bird that feeds on dead animals.
examples: A couple of *vultures* were circling over the highway.
The *vulture* waited until the coyote left.
*Vultures* clean up carcasses that would otherwise rot.

gloss: A large black bird with a harsh call.
examples: A *crow* landed on the mailbox and stared at me.
*Crows* remember faces, which is a little unsettling.
The *crow* dropped a walnut on the road so a car would crack it.

gloss: A large black bird like a crow but bigger, with a deeper call.
examples: A *raven* is much bigger than a crow, and its call is deeper.
*Ravens* nested on the cliff above the trail.
The *raven* followed us for half a mile, hoping for scraps.

gloss: A small brown and gray bird common in towns and gardens.
examples: A *sparrow* built a nest in the gutter.
*Sparrows* were fighting over crumbs on the patio.
There is always a *sparrow* or two under the feeder.

gloss: A gray city bird with a small head and a fat body.
examples: A *pigeon* was walking around the subway platform.
The old man feeds the *pigeons* in the square every morning.
A *pigeon* got into the warehouse and could not find its way out.
contrast: Two syllables, not three: PIJ-un, never pi-JEE-on. The g is soft.

gloss: A small pale pigeon, often used as a symbol of peace.
examples: A *dove* landed on the windowsill and cooed.
Two white *doves* were released at the wedding.
The *dove* is a symbol of peace in a lot of countries.
contrast: The bird rhymes with love: /dʌv/. The identically spelled past tense of dive is /doʊv/, rhyming with stove.

gloss: A common garden bird with a red or orange breast.
examples: A *robin* was pulling a worm out of the lawn.
*Robins* show up in the yard as soon as the ground thaws.
We watched a *robin* feed her chicks all afternoon.

gloss: A water bird with webbed feet and a flat bill.
examples: A *duck* and six ducklings crossed the road in front of us.
We fed the *ducks* at the pond, though the sign says not to.
He ordered roast *duck* with plum sauce.

gloss: A large white water bird with a long curved neck.
examples: A *swan* glided past us without making a sound.
Two *swans* have nested on the lake for years.
The *swan* hissed when we got too close to the nest.
contrast: The a is /ɑː/: SWAHN rhymes with on, not with man.

gloss: A flightless black and white sea bird of the southern hemisphere.
examples: The zoo just opened a new *penguin* exhibit.
*Penguins* cannot fly, but they swim beautifully.
A *penguin* waddled up to the glass and stared at my son.

gloss: A very large flightless African bird that runs fast.
examples: An *ostrich* can outrun a horse over open ground.
They raise *ostriches* on a farm outside of town.
The *ostrich* laid an egg the size of a football.

gloss: A brightly colored tropical bird with a curved beak that can copy speech.
examples: Their *parrot* says hello every time the doorbell rings.
*Parrots* can live for fifty years or more.
The *parrot* bit my finger when I got too close.

gloss: A small parrot with a long tail, often kept as a pet.
examples: She keeps two *parakeets* in a cage by the window.
The *parakeet* escaped and spent the night on the curtain rod.
A green *parakeet* was chirping in the pet store.

gloss: A large parrot with a crest that it can raise on its head.
examples: The *cockatoo* raised its crest when the dog walked in.
*Cockatoos* are loud enough to wake the neighbors.
He taught his *cockatoo* to whistle the theme song.

gloss: A big long-tailed parrot from Central and South America.
examples: A blue and gold *macaw* sat on the trainer's arm.
*Macaws* need a lot of space and a lot of attention.
The *macaw* screamed every time the phone rang.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable: muh-KAW.

gloss: A male bird with a huge fan-shaped tail of blue and green feathers.
examples: A *peacock* spread its tail right in front of the tourists.
*Peacocks* wander loose all over the hotel grounds.
The *peacock* let out that awful cry at five in the morning.

gloss: A gray and white sea bird common along coasts.
examples: A *seagull* stole a fry right out of my hand.
The *seagulls* follow the fishing boats back into the harbor.
One *seagull* landed on the roof of the car.

gloss: A sea bird of the same family as the seagull.
examples: A *gull* was riding the wind over the pier.
*Gulls* nest on the rocks at the end of the beach.
The *gull* dropped a clam on the parking lot to break it open.

gloss: A tall wading bird with long legs and a long straight bill.
examples: A *stork* was standing in the shallow water.
*Storks* nest on chimneys in a lot of old towns.
In the old story, a *stork* brings the baby.

gloss: A tall long-necked bird that lives in wetlands.
examples: A *crane* took off from the marsh as we drove by.
Thousands of *cranes* stop here on their way south.
The *crane* stood on one leg for almost ten minutes.
contrast: The same word also means a lifting machine on a building site; only context tells you which.

gloss: A wading bird with long legs and a sharp bill that spears fish.
examples: A blue *heron* was standing dead still at the edge of the pond.
*Herons* nest in the tall trees along the river.
The *heron* speared a fish and swallowed it whole.

gloss: A large water bird with a pouch under its bill for holding fish.
examples: A *pelican* dove straight into the surf.
*Pelicans* line up on the railing at the end of the pier.
The *pelican* had a fish flopping around in its pouch.

gloss: A small fast bird with pointed wings and a forked tail.
examples: A *swallow* built a mud nest under the eaves.
*Swallows* come back to the barn every April.
The *swallow* caught a bug in midair.
contrast: Spelled and said exactly like the verb swallow (to send food down your throat).

gloss: A bird that hammers holes in trees with its beak to find insects.
examples: A *woodpecker* has been hammering on the siding since dawn.
*Woodpeckers* drill holes to get at insects under the bark.
The *woodpecker* left a row of neat holes in the dead tree.

gloss: A tiny bird that hovers in front of flowers and beats its wings very fast.
examples: A *hummingbird* hovered at the feeder for a few seconds.
*Hummingbirds* beat their wings so fast you can barely see them.
We put out sugar water to bring the *hummingbirds* in.

gloss: A small yellow songbird often kept in a cage.
examples: Their *canary* sings all morning.
Miners used to carry *canaries* down into the shafts.
The *canary* stopped singing when we turned on the vacuum.
contrast: Stress on the middle syllable: kuh-NAIR-ee, not CAN-uh-ree.

gloss: A small seed-eating songbird with a short thick beak.
examples: A *finch* was picking seeds off the ground.
*Finches* took over the feeder by the garage.
The little yellow *finch* comes back every summer.

gloss: A small bright yellow finch with black markings.
examples: A *goldfinch* landed on the thistle feeder.
*Goldfinches* turn bright yellow in the spring.
We counted six *goldfinches* in the yard this morning.

gloss: A small brown bird famous for singing at night.
examples: A *nightingale* was singing somewhere in the dark.
*Nightingales* are famous for their song, not their looks.
He said the *nightingale* kept him awake half the night.

gloss: A bird that lays its eggs in other birds' nests and calls its own name.
examples: A *cuckoo* was calling from the woods.
*Cuckoos* lay their eggs in other birds' nests.
The clock has a little wooden *cuckoo* that pops out on the hour.

gloss: A noisy black and white bird with a long tail.
examples: A *magpie* carried off a piece of foil from the trash.
*Magpies* are smart enough to recognize themselves in a mirror.
The *magpie* sat on the fence, chattering at the cat.

gloss: A dark speckled bird that flies in huge flocks and copies other sounds.
examples: A *starling* was picking at the grass by the curb.
Thousands of *starlings* wheeled over the field at dusk.
The *starling* can imitate a car alarm almost perfectly.

gloss: A loud, bold bird of the crow family, often blue in North America.
examples: A blue *jay* chased the squirrel off the feeder.
*Jays* scream when there is a hawk around.
The *jay* buried an acorn in the flower bed.

gloss: A common black songbird.
examples: A *blackbird* was singing on the fence post.
*Blackbirds* fill the marsh in the spring.
The *blackbird* flew off as soon as I opened the door.

gloss: A small North American songbird with bright blue feathers.
examples: A *bluebird* took over the box we put up last year.
*Bluebirds* are back, so spring must be close.
The *bluebird* sat on the wire for a long time.

gloss: A North American songbird; the male is bright red with a crest.
examples: A male *cardinal* is impossible to miss against the snow.
*Cardinals* come to the feeder all winter.
The *cardinal* was singing from the top of the maple.

gloss: A very small brown bird with a short upright tail and a loud song.
examples: A *wren* built a nest in the flowerpot.
*Wrens* are tiny, but they are unbelievably loud.
The *wren* scolded me the whole time I was on the porch.
contrast: The w is silent: REN, one syllable.

gloss: A brown field bird that sings while flying high in the air.
examples: A *lark* rose straight up over the field, singing.
*Larks* nest right on the ground.
We heard a *lark* long before we saw it.

gloss: A brightly colored bird that dives into water to catch fish.
examples: A *kingfisher* was perched on a branch over the creek.
*Kingfishers* hunt by dropping straight into the water.
The *kingfisher* rattled as it flew downstream.

gloss: A small black and white sea bird with a large brightly striped bill.
examples: We took a boat out to see the *puffins*.
A *puffin* landed with three fish in its beak.
*Puffins* nest in burrows on the cliffs.

gloss: A very large sea bird with long narrow wings that glides for hours.
examples: An *albatross* followed the ship for two days.
*Albatrosses* can glide for hours without flapping.
The *albatross* has the longest wingspan of any bird.

gloss: A very large vulture of the American mountains.
examples: A wild *condor* passed right over the canyon rim.
There were only a couple dozen *condors* left in the wild.
The *condor* is slowly coming back from near extinction.

gloss: A broad-winged bird of prey; in American usage often a vulture.
examples: A *buzzard* was picking at something on the shoulder of the road.
*Buzzards* were circling over the field all afternoon.
The *buzzard* took off when the truck came around the bend.
contrast: In American English a buzzard is usually a vulture; in British English it is a kind of hawk.

gloss: A large fish-eating bird of prey found near water.
examples: An *osprey* dropped feet first into the lake and came up with a fish.
*Ospreys* build huge nests on top of power poles.
The *osprey* has been fishing this stretch of river all summer.

gloss: A large flightless Australian bird, second in height only to the ostrich.
examples: An *emu* got loose from the farm and walked down the highway.
*Emus* are the second tallest birds in the world.
The *emu* pecked at my shoelaces.

gloss: A small flightless New Zealand bird with a long thin bill.
examples: A *kiwi* is about the size of a chicken and cannot fly.
*Kiwis* come out at night and hunt by smell.
We never saw a wild *kiwi*, only one at the sanctuary.
contrast: The same word names the green fruit; the bird sense came first.

gloss: A tropical American bird with an enormous colorful bill.
examples: A *toucan* landed in the tree above our table.
*Toucans* use that huge bill to reach fruit on thin branches.
The *toucan* tossed the berry into the air and caught it.
contrast: Sounds like the words two can: TOO-kan.

gloss: A large bird raised for meat, with a bare head and a fanned tail.
examples: We roast a *turkey* every Thanksgiving.
Wild *turkeys* walk through the yard most mornings.
There is still some *turkey* left in the fridge.

gloss: An adult male chicken.
examples: The *rooster* starts crowing around four in the morning.
They keep one *rooster* and a dozen hens.
Two *roosters* in the same pen is asking for a fight.
contrast: American English says rooster; British English usually says cock or cockerel.

gloss: An adult female chicken, or the female of some other birds.
examples: One *hen* is laying an egg almost every day.
The *hens* got out and were all over the driveway.
A *hen* will sit on the eggs for about three weeks.

gloss: A very young bird, especially a young chicken.
examples: A *chick* poked its head out of the shell.
All twelve *chicks* hatched over two days.
The mother bird kept bringing worms back to the *chick*.

gloss: A young duck.
examples: A *duckling* was trailing behind the others.
Nine *ducklings* followed their mother into the water.
The *duckling* was all fuzz and feet.

gloss: A young goose.
examples: A *gosling* was grazing on the lawn by the pond.
The geese hissed whenever anyone got near the *goslings*.
That *gosling* is almost as big as its parents now.
contrast: The o is /ɑː/, not the /uː/ of goose: GAHZ-ling.

gloss: A young swan.
examples: A *cygnet* is gray for the first year.
The pair had five *cygnets* riding on their backs.
The *cygnet* stayed close to its mother the whole time.
contrast: Sounds exactly like signet (a signet ring): the c is /s/ and the g is hard.

gloss: A male duck.
examples: The *drake* has the green head; the female is brown.
Two *drakes* were chasing each other across the pond.
A *drake* landed in the decoys about twenty yards out.

gloss: A male goose.
examples: The *gander* hissed and came at me with his neck out.
One *gander* can guard a whole yard.
The *ganders* were fighting over territory by the water.

gloss: A gray North American songbird that imitates other birds and sounds.
examples: A *mockingbird* sang outside my window until two in the morning.
*Mockingbirds* can copy car alarms and cell phones.
The *mockingbird* dive-bombed the cat.

gloss: A small North American bird with a black cap, named for its call.
examples: A *chickadee* grabbed one seed and flew off with it.
*Chickadees* stay all winter, even in the cold.
The *chickadee* landed right on my hand.

gloss: A diving water bird of northern lakes with a haunting call.
examples: A *loon* called out across the lake at sunset.
*Loons* dive and stay under for a surprisingly long time.
We watched a *loon* carry its chick on its back.

gloss: A large flightless bird that died out in the seventeenth century.
examples: The *dodo* has been extinct for over three hundred years.
*Dodos* had no natural predators until sailors arrived.
The museum has a model of a *dodo* in the entryway.

gloss: A bird that lives on or near the ocean.
examples: A *seabird* was riding the wind above the cliffs.
*Seabirds* nest by the thousands on that island.
The oil spill killed every *seabird* along the coast.

gloss: A bird known for its musical call.
examples: A *songbird* woke us up at first light.
*Songbirds* are disappearing from a lot of the country.
The cat has killed more than one *songbird* this summer.

gloss: A bird that swims and lives on water, such as a duck or a goose.
examples: The refuge protects *waterfowl* on their way south.
A single *waterfowl* was left on the frozen pond.
Hunting *waterfowl* here requires a separate permit.
contrast: The plural is normally waterfowl, unchanged — not waterfowls.

gloss: Birds such as chickens and turkeys kept for eggs and meat, or their meat.
examples: The farm sells *poultry* and eggs at the market.
*Poultry* is cheaper than beef right now.
He does not eat red meat, only fish and *poultry*.
contrast: Uncountable: poultry is, never a poultry or poultries.

gloss: A bird kept for meat and eggs, or a wild bird hunted for food.
examples: The pond was full of wild *fowl*.
They keep a few *fowl* out behind the barn.
The recipe works with any kind of *fowl*.
contrast: Sounds exactly like foul (unfair, disgusting), and the plural is usually fowl, unchanged.

gloss: A bird that hunts other animals, such as a hawk, eagle, or owl.
examples: A *raptor* was perched on the light pole over the interstate.
*Raptors* have hooked beaks and very sharp talons.
The center takes in injured *raptors* and releases them.

gloss: A bird that kills and eats other animals.
examples: A *bird of prey* was working the field along the fence line.
Hawks, eagles, and owls are all *birds of prey*.
The *bird of prey* dropped on the mouse without a sound.
contrast: The plural is birds of prey — the s goes on bird, not on prey.

gloss: One of the light growths that cover a bird's body.
examples: A single *feather* drifted down onto the deck.
The pillow is stuffed with duck *feathers*.
She found a blue jay *feather* on the trail.
contrast: The ea is short: FE-thur, rhyming with weather, not with either.

gloss: One of the two limbs a bird uses to fly.
examples: The bird broke a *wing* hitting the window.
It spread its *wings* and took off.
One *wing* was still bandaged when we let it go.

gloss: The distance from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.
examples: That eagle had a six-foot *wingspan*.
A condor has the biggest *wingspan* of any bird on the continent.
Their *wingspans* can reach almost ten feet.

gloss: The hard pointed mouth part of a bird.
examples: The bird had a worm in its *beak*.
Parrots crack seeds with their *beaks*.
It cleaned its feathers with the tip of its *beak*.

gloss: A bird's beak, especially a flat wide one.
examples: A duck's *bill* is flat and wide.
The pelican's *bill* holds more than its stomach does.
Some birds have long, curved *bills* for reaching into flowers.
contrast: The same word also means a bill you pay and, in American English, a banknote (a ten-dollar bill).

gloss: A sharp curved nail on a bird's or animal's foot.
examples: The bird gripped the branch with one *claw*.
Its *claws* left scratches on the wooden perch.
The chick's *claw* was barely the size of my fingernail.

gloss: A claw on a bird of prey.
examples: The hawk sank a *talon* into the rabbit.
Owls carry prey in their *talons*.
One *talon* was broken off at the tip.

gloss: A tuft of feathers on top of a bird's head.
examples: The bird raised its *crest* when it got excited.
Cardinals have a pointed *crest* on the head.
Both *crests* went up the moment the dog appeared.

gloss: The red fleshy growth on top of a chicken's head.
examples: The rooster's *comb* is bright red.
Frostbite can damage a hen's *comb*.
Different breeds have very different *combs*.
contrast: The b is silent: KOHM, exactly like a comb for your hair.

gloss: All the feathers covering a bird.
examples: The male's *plumage* is much brighter than the female's.
Winter *plumage* is duller and better for hiding.
Its *plumage* was still wet from the rain.
contrast: Uncountable: bright plumage, never a plumage or plumages.

gloss: The soft fine feathers under a bird's outer feathers.
examples: The chicks are covered in soft gray *down*.
The jacket is filled with goose *down*.
*Down* is warmer than any synthetic filling.
contrast: Uncountable: some down, never a down or downs. Spelled like the direction word down.

gloss: A large stiff feather, or a pen made from one.
examples: A single *quill* had fallen out of the wing.
People used to write with goose *quills*.
The *quill* was stiff and hollow at the base.

gloss: The feathers at the back end of a bird, used for steering.
examples: The bird flicked its *tail* and flew off.
Peacocks spread their *tails* to show off.
A long *tail* helps a bird steer in the air.
contrast: Sounds exactly like tale (a story).

gloss: The front of a bird's body, or the meat from it.
examples: The robin has an orange *breast*.
We grilled two chicken *breasts* for dinner.
The bird's *breast* was streaked with brown.
contrast: One syllable with a short e: BREST, rhyming with rest.

gloss: The muscular part of a bird's stomach that grinds up food.
examples: A bird grinds its food in the *gizzard*.
She saves the *gizzards* for gravy.
The *gizzard* was full of small stones.

gloss: The round object with a shell that a bird lays and a chick grows inside.
examples: The hen laid an *egg* in the corner of the coop.
There were four blue *eggs* in the nest.
The *egg* hatched sometime overnight.

gloss: The thin hard outer covering of an egg.
examples: The *eggshell* cracked from the inside.
There were bits of *eggshell* all over the nest.
*Eggshells* are good for the compost pile.

gloss: The yellow part inside an egg.
examples: The *yolk* feeds the chick before it hatches.
Break the *yolk* and it runs everywhere.
Two of the eggs had double *yolks*.
contrast: The l is silent: YOHK, exactly like yoke.

gloss: The seasonal journey birds make from one region to another.
examples: The fall *migration* starts in late August.
Their yearly *migration* covers eight thousand miles.
Storms can throw whole *migrations* off course.

gloss: The act or manner of flying through the air.
examples: The owl's *flight* is completely silent.
We tracked the bird's *flight* until it went behind the trees.
A pelican's *flight* looks awkward until it hits the water.

gloss: A branch, bar, or place where birds settle to sleep.
examples: The chickens went back to the *roost* at dusk.
Crows use the same *roost* every night.
There were a hundred birds on that one *roost*.

gloss: The period when a bird sheds old feathers and grows new ones.
examples: The annual *molt* leaves them looking half bald.
Most ducks go through one *molt* a year.
After the *molt*, the feathers come in bright again.
contrast: American spelling molt; British English writes moult, said the same way.

gloss: A short high sound made by a small bird.
examples: There was a *chirp* from somewhere in the bushes.
You could hear the *chirps* of the chicks inside the box.
One sharp *chirp* and the whole flock lifted off.

gloss: A short high sound made by a small bird.
examples: A *tweet* came from the nest above the door.
The little *tweets* got louder when the mother came back.
I heard one *tweet* and then nothing.
contrast: Far more common now as an online post, but the bird sound is the original meaning.

gloss: The musical sound made by singing birds.
examples: The morning was full of *birdsong*.
*Birdsong* woke me up before my alarm did.
You can barely hear the *birdsong* over the traffic.
contrast: Uncountable: a lot of birdsong, never a birdsong or birdsongs.

gloss: The characteristic cry of a particular bird, or a device that imitates it.
examples: He can imitate almost any *birdcall*.
The app identifies *birdcalls* from a recording.
That *birdcall* belongs to a barred owl.

gloss: The low call of an owl.
examples: A *hoot* came from the woods behind the house.
We counted four *hoots* and then silence.
The owl gave one long *hoot* and flew off.

gloss: The harsh cry of a crow or rook.
examples: A single *caw* echoed across the field.
The *caws* got louder as more crows arrived.
One *caw* from the lookout and the flock was gone.

gloss: The sound a duck makes.
examples: We heard a *quack* from the reeds.
The *quacks* got frantic when the bread came out.
A loud *quack* woke the whole campsite.

gloss: The short low sound a hen makes.
examples: There was a soft *cluck* from inside the coop.
The *clucks* stopped the second the door opened.
A hen gives a low *cluck* to call her chicks.

gloss: A loud harsh cry made by a bird.
examples: The parrot let out a *squawk* that made everyone jump.
The gulls answered with *squawks* from all over the roof.
She heard a *squawk* and found the cat under the birdcage.

gloss: A loud, high, unpleasant cry.
examples: The owl let out a *screech* that carried across the whole valley.
The *screeches* went on most of the night.
That *screech* is a barn owl, not a person.

gloss: The soft low sound a dove or pigeon makes.
examples: There was a soft *coo* from the ledge above the window.
The *coos* of the pigeons carried down the alley.
He heard a low *coo* and found a dove on the sill.

gloss: A bird that has just come out of its egg.
examples: The *hatchling* was blind and completely bald.
All six *hatchlings* need feeding every twenty minutes.
A *hatchling* cannot keep itself warm.

gloss: A young bird that has just grown its flight feathers.
examples: A *fledgling* was hopping around the yard, unable to fly yet.
*Fledglings* often look abandoned when the parents are close by.
The *fledgling* finally made it up onto the fence.

gloss: The hobby of looking for and identifying wild birds.
examples: He got into *birdwatching* after he retired.
*Birdwatching* is a lot more work than it sounds.
We do a little *birdwatching* whenever we are at the coast.
contrast: Uncountable: some birdwatching, never a birdwatching.

gloss: Someone whose hobby is finding and identifying wild birds.
examples: A *birder* stopped us on the trail to point out an owl.
*Birders* line up at the marsh before sunrise.
She is a serious *birder* with a life list of six hundred.

gloss: The scientific study of birds.
examples: He studied *ornithology* in graduate school.
*Ornithology* has changed a lot since DNA testing.
She teaches *ornithology* at the state university.
contrast: Stress on the third syllable: or-nuh-THAH-luh-jee, and the th is the sound in thin.

gloss: A scientist who studies birds.
examples: An *ornithologist* came out to band the chicks.
Two *ornithologists* spent the summer counting nests.
The *ornithologist* identified the bird from a five-second recording.

gloss: A large cage or building where birds are kept.
examples: The zoo's *aviary* is under a huge net.
You can walk right through the *aviary* and the birds land on you.
Both *aviaries* were closed for cleaning.

gloss: A cage for keeping a pet bird.
examples: The *birdcage* hangs in the corner by the window.
He cleans the *birdcage* every Saturday.
There were two empty *birdcages* in the garage.

gloss: A small wooden box put up outdoors for wild birds to nest in.
examples: We nailed a *birdhouse* to the fence post.
Something is nesting in the *birdhouse* already.
He builds *birdhouses* out of scrap lumber.

ru: птичья купальня (чаша с водой в саду)
gloss: A shallow basin of water in a yard for birds to drink and wash in.
examples: The *birdbath* freezes solid in January.
Three sparrows were splashing around in the *birdbath*.
Change the water in the *birdbath* every couple of days.

gloss: A mixture of seeds sold as food for birds.
examples: We are out of *birdseed* again.
The squirrels get more *birdseed* than the birds do.
A twenty-pound bag of *birdseed* lasts about a month.
contrast: Uncountable: a bag of birdseed, never a birdseed or birdseeds.

gloss: A container hung outdoors that holds seed for wild birds.
examples: A bear knocked the *bird feeder* off the pole.
We keep two *bird feeders* going all winter.
The *bird feeder* is empty again.

gloss: A small building or pen where chickens are kept.
examples: He locks the *coop* at night to keep the raccoons out.
Both *coops* need new roofs.
The hens go back into the *coop* on their own at dusk.
contrast: One syllable, KOOP. Do not read it as co-op, a cooperative, which is KOH-ahp.

gloss: The solid waste that birds and small animals leave behind.
examples: There were *droppings* all over the porch railing.
Bird *droppings* will eat right through car paint.
He scraped the *droppings* off the windshield.
contrast: Always plural in form: the droppings are, never a dropping.

gloss: The V-shaped bone in a bird's chest, pulled apart for luck.
examples: The kids fought over who got to pull the *wishbone*.
We dried the *wishbone* on the windowsill.
Two *wishbones* were still sitting on the counter.

gloss: The lower part of a cooked bird's leg.
examples: He ate three *drumsticks* and half the mashed potatoes.
The *drumstick* is the lower part of the leg.
Kids always go for the *drumsticks* first.
contrast: The same word also means the stick you hit a drum with.

gloss: A figure dressed in old clothes, put in a field to frighten birds away.
examples: The *scarecrow* in the garden has not fooled a single crow.
They put up two *scarecrows* along the corn rows.
The *scarecrow* was wearing my old jacket.

gloss: The order of rank in a group, originally among hens in a flock.
examples: There is a clear *pecking order* in the henhouse.
New hires figure out the *pecking order* pretty fast.
Every team develops a *pecking order*, whether anyone admits it or not.
